panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Gross cardiac specimen showing HLHS with intact ventricular septum: atretic atrioventricular junction with blind-ending vestibule and labeled hypoplastic left ventricle, directly captioned as HLHS phenotype. B: Gross cardiac specimen showing HLHS: imperforate mitral valve (= imperforate mitral valve synonym for mitral atresia) with hypoplastic left ventricle. C: Gross cardiac specimen showing HLHS with stenotic mitral valve and hypoplastic left ventricle lined by dense fibroelastosis, apex-forming right ventricle.
panels.attribution_text: Anderson et al. What Is the Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome?. Journal of cardiovascular development and disease 2023. doi:10.3390/jcdd10040133. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: The images show the sequence of development of the mitral valve in the setting of hypoplastic left heart when the syndrome is defined on the basis of an intact ventricular septum. In panel (A), the atrioventricular connection had been formed, as evidenced by the presence of a blind-ending vestibule in the floor of the left atrium, but has become atretic. Panel (B) shows an imperforate mitral valve closing off a perforate left atrioventricular junction, while panel (C) shows a stenotic valve. Note that, in the setting of the stenotic valve, the cavity of the hypoplastic left ventricle is lined by a dense layer of fibroelastosis. Such elastosis is lacking in the hypoplastic left ventricles seen in panels (A,B).
in_text_mentions: ion of the Norwood sequence for surgical palliation [10] shows a spectrum of malformation of change in the setting of an intact ventricular septum [3,4]. These sequential changes are to be seen with regard to all the components of the left side of the heart when the left ventricle is hypoplastic in the setting of an intact ventricular septum. They are not seen in the same sequence when hypoplasia of the ventricle is found with either atrioventricular or ventricular septal defects. Thus, when the ventricular septum is intact, the mitral valve can be atretic, imperforate, or stenotic (Figure 4).

Caption attributes to combined aortic and mitral stenosis subgroup of HLHS; LV still hypoplastic but larger than atresia variant with dense fibroelastotic lining.

panels.figure_caption: The images show the phenotypic features of the three subgroups of lesions that can be identified in the setting of hypoplasia of the left heart when the ventricular septum is intact. Panel (A) shows the grossly hypoplastic ventricle found when there is combined aortic and mitral atresia. The ventricle is no more than a slit on the diaphragmatic surface of the ventricular mass. It is found by dissecting between the delimiting coronary arteries. Panel (B) shows the features of aortic atresia with mitral stenosis, while panel (C) shows the findings with combined aortic and mitral stenosis. The left ventricle is larger in the setting of mitral stenosis, but is characterised by its dense fibroelastotic lining.
in_text_mentions: The overall findings from the hearts collected together in archives created prior to the advent of surgical correction support the existence of the phenotypical subsets highlighted in the European guidelines [8]. Thus, the hearts can be grouped together into subsets of combined aortic and mitral atresia, aortic atresia with mitral stenosis, and combined aortic and mitral stenosis (Figure 5).

panels.figure_caption: Severe aortic valve stenosis is shown in panel (A) from a parasternal long-axis view. Severe mitral valve hypoplasia with evident endocardial fibroelastosis of the left ventricle in panel (B). Four-chamber view in panel (C) shows a double inlet right ventricle with virtually absent left ventricle. Mitral atresia in panel (D,E) is associated with dysplasia of the tricuspid valve, with moderate regurgitation. Aortic valve atresia with severely hypoplastic ascending aorta is shown in panel (F). panels.rationale: Real patient echocardiogram (apical 4-chamber view) from a case report titled 'Single Ventricle With Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome in a 22-Year-Old Male'. The caption describes a single ventricle with a rudimentary right ventricle, and the in-text explicitly states 'hypoplastic left ventricle' and 'single ventricle', supporting attribution to hypoplastic_left_heart_syndrome with a diminutive left ventricle. The dominant single-ventricle morphology is the classic echo manifestation of HLHS; survival to age 22 without staged palliation is rare but does not make the imaging finding atypical. No skin, ethnicity, or staging information is applicable.
